specStatements.text: Energy is stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up the system. This is called internal energy.
Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up a system.
Heating changes the energy stored within the system by increasing the energy of the particles that make up the system. This either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state.
If the temperature of the system increases, the increase in temperature depends on the mass of the substance heated, the type of material and the energy input to the system.
The following equation applies:
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
[∆E = m c ∆θ]
change in thermal energy, ∆ E, in joules, J
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
specific heat capacity, c, in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C
temperature change, ∆ θ, in degrees Celsius, °C.
The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
If a change of state happens:
The energy needed for a substance to change state is called latent heat. When a change of state occurs, the energy supplied changes the energy stored (internal energy) but not the temperature.
The specific latent heat of a substance is the amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.
energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat
[E = m L]
energy, E, in joules, J
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
specific latent heat, L, in joules per kilogram, J/kg
Specific latent heat of fusion – change of state from solid to liquid
Specific latent heat of vaporisation – change of state from liquid to vapour
Students should be able to interpret heating and cooling graphs that include changes of state.
Students should be able to distinguish between specific heat capacity and specific latent heat.

concepts.definition: The energy stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up that system. It is a store held by the particles, not a fluid that enters or leaves the system.
The energy the particles have because they are moving, vibrating or rotating. It is one of the two contributions to internal energy, and it is the contribution linked to temperature.

The energy stored because of the positions of the particles relative to one another and the forces between them. It is the second contribution to internal energy, and it is the store that changes during a change of state.
An energy transfer that increases the energy of the particles that make up a system. The result is either a rise in the temperature of the system or a change of state.
change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ. It applies when heating or cooling changes the temperature of a substance.
Change in thermal energy, ∆E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; temperature change, ∆θ, is in degrees Celsius, °C.
Specific heat capacity, c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, because it is an energy quoted for each kilogram and for each degree Celsius of temperature change.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
A change between solid, liquid and vapour in which the substance stays the same substance. While it happens the temperature does not change, even though energy is still being transferred.
The energy needed for a substance to change state. It changes the energy stored (internal energy) of the substance but not its temperature.
The amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of a substance with no change in temperature. Energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, or E = m L.
Energy, E, is in joules, J; mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, is in joules per kilogram, J/kg. No temperature unit appears because the temperature does not change.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from solid to liquid, that is for melting, and in reverse for freezing.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from liquid to vapour, that is for boiling, and in reverse for condensing.

A graph of temperature against time for a substance heated or cooled at a steady rate. Sloping sections show the temperature changing within one state; flat sections show a change of state, where energy is still transferred but the temperature is constant.

misconceptions.question: Two beakers of water are at the same temperature but one holds twice as much water. Do they store the same internal energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. The larger sample has twice as many particles, so its total kinetic and potential energy, and therefore its internal energy, is greater.
misconceptions.misconception: Internal energy is the same thing as temperature, so two things at the same temperature must store the same energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature is the only number students routinely attach to a hot object, and 'hot' and 'full of energy' are used interchangeably in everyday speech.
misconceptions.correction: Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles. Internal energy is the total for all of them, so it depends on how many particles there are as well as how fast they move.

misconceptions.question: What two energy stores add up to the internal energy of a system?
misconceptions.correct: The kinetic energy and the potential energy of all the particles that make up the system.
misconceptions.misconception: Internal energy is just the kinetic energy of the particles, because internal energy is about particle motion.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Particle animations and models show particles moving, but nothing on screen represents the energy stored in the forces between them.
misconceptions.correction: Particles also attract one another, so energy is stored in their positions. That potential energy is part of internal energy and is the part that changes during melting and boiling.

misconceptions.question: A beaker of melting ice is heated steadily. Does its temperature rise?
misconceptions.correct: No. While the ice is melting the temperature stays at 0 °C; the energy produces the change of state instead.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating a system always makes its temperature go up, so a thermometer must read higher whenever energy is supplied.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every everyday example of heating (a kettle, an oven, a radiator) does raise a temperature, so the exception is never met.
misconceptions.correction: Heating increases the energy of the particles. That either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state, not always the former.

misconceptions.question: 1 kg of water and 1 kg of cooking oil are each given 20 000 J. Do they warm by the same amount?
misconceptions.correct: No. The oil warms more, because oil has a lower specific heat capacity than water.
misconceptions.misconception: Equal masses given equal energy must reach equal temperatures, because the energy input is the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat energy input as the only cause of a temperature rise and overlook the type of material, which is invisible in the numbers given.
misconceptions.correction: The increase in temperature depends on the mass, the type of material and the energy input. Two different materials respond differently to the same energy.

misconceptions.question: What exactly does a specific heat capacity of 4200 J/kg °C tell you?
misconceptions.correct: 4200 J are needed to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the energy needed to raise the temperature of the whole sample by one degree Celsius, whatever its mass.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'specific' is not read as 'per kilogram', so the mass condition drops out of the definition.
misconceptions.correction: 'Specific' means per kilogram. The value is quoted for exactly one kilogram, which is why mass is multiplied in when ∆E = m c ∆θ is used.

misconceptions.question: Energy keeps being supplied to boiling water. Why does the thermometer reading stop rising?
misconceptions.correct: The energy supplied is changing the state of the water, increasing the internal energy without raising the temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: As long as energy is still supplied the temperature must keep creeping up, so a steady reading means the energy supply has stopped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy in is linked directly to temperature out, with no separate store for the change of state.
misconceptions.correction: During a change of state the energy supplied goes into the potential energy store of the particles, separating them. The temperature stays constant until the change of state is complete.

misconceptions.question: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of fusion describe?
misconceptions.correct: The change from solid to liquid, that is melting.
misconceptions.misconception: Fusion means the substance is being turned into a gas, so latent heat of fusion is the one used for boiling.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Fusion' sounds like intense heat (nuclear fusion, fusing metals), so it is attached to the hottest change of state a student can think of.
misconceptions.correction: Fusion here means melting: solid to liquid. Liquid to vapour is described by the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

misconceptions.question: A heating graph has a flat section. Is energy still being transferred to the substance during it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Energy is still being supplied; it is producing a change of state rather than a temperature rise.
misconceptions.misconception: A flat section means nothing is happening, so no energy is being transferred during it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A horizontal line is read as 'no change at all' rather than 'no change in the quantity on the y-axis'.
misconceptions.correction: Only the temperature is unchanged. The substance is melting or boiling, and the length of the flat section shows how much energy that took.

misconceptions.question: What are the units of specific latent heat?
misconceptions.misconception: Specific latent heat is measured in J/kg °C, the same units as specific heat capacity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are called 'specific', so the more familiar unit is carried across without checking what the quantity means.
misconceptions.correction: There is no temperature change during a change of state, so no 'per degree Celsius' appears. Specific latent heat is simply joules per kilogram.

misconceptions.question: Water is heated from 20 °C to 60 °C. What value of ∆θ goes into ∆E = m c ∆θ?
misconceptions.misconception: ∆θ is the final temperature, so 60 °C should be substituted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The final reading is the number the thermometer shows at the end, and the symbol ∆ is skimmed over rather than read as 'change in'.
misconceptions.correction: ∆ means 'change in'. Subtract the starting temperature from the final temperature before substituting.

misconceptions.question: A 250 g block is used in ∆E = m c ∆θ. What number should be substituted for m?
misconceptions.correct: 0.25, because mass must be in kilograms.
misconceptions.misconception: The mass can be substituted as 250, since that is the number given in the question.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Grams are the everyday laboratory unit, and the substitution is done before the units are checked.
misconceptions.correction: Mass, m, in these equations is in kilograms. Divide a mass in grams by 1000 before substituting, or the answer comes out 1000 times too large.

misconceptions.question: Substance X has a higher specific heat capacity than substance Y. For the same mass and the same energy input, which warms up more?
misconceptions.correct: Substance Y, because less energy is needed for each degree Celsius of temperature rise.
misconceptions.misconception: A higher specific heat capacity means the substance heats up more quickly, because it has a greater capacity for heating.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'High capacity' is read as 'good at getting hot' rather than 'needs a lot of energy per degree'.
misconceptions.correction: A high specific heat capacity means more energy is needed per kilogram per degree Celsius, so for the same energy input the temperature rise is smaller.

misconceptions.question: How much energy is needed to melt 2 kg of ice already at 0 °C?
misconceptions.correct: E = m L: multiply the mass by the specific latent heat of fusion.
misconceptions.misconception: A temperature change term is still needed, so the calculation should be mass × specific latent heat × temperature change.
misconceptions.whyItArises: ∆E = m c ∆θ is met first and is then used as the template for every thermal calculation.
misconceptions.correction: There is no temperature change during a change of state, so there is no ∆θ to include. The equation is simply E = m L.

misconceptions.question: What is stored inside a hot object?
misconceptions.correct: Internal energy, stored by the particles that make up the object.
misconceptions.misconception: A hot object contains heat, a substance that has flowed in and is now held inside it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday speech treats heat as a fluid: 'let the heat out', 'the heat in the room', 'keep the heat in'.
misconceptions.correction: Heating is the transfer, not the store. What the object stores is internal energy, held by its own particles.

misconceptions.question: Which energy store of the particles increases while a solid melts?
misconceptions.correct: The potential energy store, because the particles are pulled further apart against the forces between them.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles must be speeding up, so it is their kinetic energy that increases during melting.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Energy in is equated with faster particles, which is the only mechanism most students have been shown.
misconceptions.correction: Faster particles would mean a higher temperature, and the temperature is constant during melting. The energy goes into the potential energy store instead.

misconceptions.question: Does the internal energy of a substance change while it is boiling?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The energy supplied increases the internal energy even though the temperature is constant.
misconceptions.misconception: If the temperature is not changing then the internal energy is not changing either.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Internal energy and temperature are treated as the same quantity, so a steady thermometer reading is read as a steady energy store.
misconceptions.correction: Internal energy includes the potential energy of the particles. During a change of state that part rises while temperature, which tracks kinetic energy, stays the same.

misconceptions.question: How do specific heat capacity and specific latent heat differ?
misconceptions.correct: Specific heat capacity is the energy per kilogram per degree Celsius of temperature change; specific latent heat is the energy per kilogram to change state with no temperature change.
misconceptions.misconception: They are two names for the same quantity, so either can be used in any thermal calculation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are 'specific' properties, both are quoted per kilogram, and both appear in similar-looking equations.
misconceptions.correction: Use c and ∆E = m c ∆θ when the temperature changes; use L and E = m L when the state changes at constant temperature.

misconceptions.question: What are the units of specific heat capacity?
misconceptions.correct: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C.
misconceptions.misconception: Specific heat capacity is measured in joules per kilogram, J/kg.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 'per kilogram' part is remembered from the word 'specific' and the temperature condition is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: The definition fixes both conditions: one kilogram and one degree Celsius. So the unit carries both, J/kg °C.

misconceptions.question: A specific latent heat is 330 000 J/kg. How is it used for a mass of 0.30 kg?
misconceptions.misconception: Because the value is quoted 'per kilogram', the mass should be divided into it rather than multiplied by it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'per' is read as an instruction to divide, and with a mass below one kilogram dividing gives a bigger number, which feels like the safer answer.
misconceptions.correction: 'Per kilogram' states the value for each kilogram, so for m kilograms you multiply by m. The same applies to specific heat capacity in ∆E = m c ∆θ.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the internal energy of a system?

options.text: The energy stored inside the system by its own particles
options.rationale: Energy is stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up the system, and that store is called internal energy.

options.text: The temperature the system reaches when it is heated
options.rationale: Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles, not to the total energy they store.

options.text: The heat that flowed in and is now held inside
options.rationale: Heat is the transfer, not a substance that can be held. What is held is internal energy.

options.text: The energy the system gives out to its surroundings
options.rationale: That describes an energy transfer away from the system, not the store held inside it.

mcqs.stem: Internal energy is the total of which two energy stores of the particles in a system?

options.text: The chemical energy and the thermal energy of all the particles
options.rationale: Chemical energy is stored in bonds between atoms and is not one of the two stores named in the definition.

options.text: The kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particles
options.rationale: Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.

options.text: The kinetic energy of every one of the particles, only
options.rationale: Leaving out the potential energy misses the store that changes during a change of state.

options.text: The kinetic energy stored as the particles move about
options.rationale: Student believes internal energy is only the particles' kinetic energy, ignoring potential energy.

mcqs.stem: Where does the potential energy part of a system's internal energy come from?

options.text: From the speeds at which the particles are moving about inside
options.rationale: Speed sets the kinetic energy of the particles, which is the other contribution to internal energy.

options.text: From the height of the system above the floor of the laboratory
options.rationale: That is the gravitational potential energy of the whole object, not a store held by its particles.

options.text: From the positions of particles and the forces between them
options.rationale: Particles attract one another, so energy is stored in how they are arranged; that is the potential energy part.

options.text: From the temperature the system has been raised to
options.rationale: Temperature is linked to average kinetic energy; it is not the source of the potential energy store.

mcqs.stem: Heating a system increases the energy of the particles that make it up. Which pair of outcomes does the specification give for this?

options.text: It always raises the temperature of the system, without exception
options.rationale: A melting or boiling substance is being heated with no rise in temperature at all.

options.text: It raises the temperature and it always changes state as well
options.rationale: The two outcomes are alternatives; warming water from 20 °C to 30 °C changes no state.

options.text: It raises the pressure or else it produces a change of state
options.rationale: Pressure is not one of the two outcomes given for heating a system in this part of the specification.

options.text: It raises the temperature or it produces a change of state
options.rationale: This is what the specification states: heating either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state.

mcqs.stem: A beaker of ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater until all the ice has melted. What does the heating do during that time?

options.text: It raises the temperature of the ice steadily as it melts
options.rationale: Heating does not always raise a temperature; while ice melts the reading stays at 0 °C.

options.text: It increases the energy stored and produces a change of state
options.rationale: The energy supplied increases the energy of the particles and produces the change of state from solid to liquid.

options.text: The energy stored stays the same as the temperature holds steady
options.rationale: Constant melting temperature is taken to mean internal (stored) energy cannot change.

options.text: It has no effect until the ice reaches its melting point
options.rationale: The ice is already at its melting point, so the energy supplied is used immediately.

mcqs.stem: When a substance is heated and its temperature increases, the size of that increase depends on which three things?

options.text: The volume, the type of material and the total time of heating
options.rationale: The specification names mass rather than volume, and energy input rather than time.

options.text: The mass, the final temperature and the energy supplied
options.rationale: The starting temperature does not fix the size of the rise; the type of material does.

options.text: The mass, the type of material and the energy input to it
options.rationale: These are the three factors the specification lists for the increase in temperature.

options.text: The mass, the energy input and the type of container
options.rationale: Believing only mass and energy matter, the student ignores material and adds an irrelevant factor.

mcqs.stem: 1 kg of water and 1 kg of cooking oil are each supplied with 20 000 J. The oil ends up much hotter than the water. Why?

options.text: Equal masses given equal energy must reach equal temperatures
options.rationale: The type of material matters as well as the mass and the energy input, so the rises differ.

options.text: The oil has a much higher specific heat capacity than water
options.rationale: A higher specific heat capacity gives a smaller rise for the same energy, not a larger one.

options.text: The oil is thicker, so the heater warms it up quickly
options.rationale: Thickness is not one of the factors that fixes the temperature increase of a heated substance.

options.text: Oil has a lower specific heat capacity than the water does
options.rationale: The increase in temperature depends on the type of material; oil needs less energy per kilogram per degree Celsius.

mcqs.stem: Which word equation for the change in thermal energy is the one given in the specification?

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change
options.rationale: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ.

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × the final temperature
options.rationale: ∆θ means the change in temperature, so the final reading cannot be substituted straight into the equation.

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific latent heat × the temperature change
options.rationale: Specific latent heat belongs to changes of state, where there is no temperature change.

options.text: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity ÷ the temperature change
options.rationale: The three quantities are multiplied; dividing would make a bigger temperature change need less energy.

mcqs.stem: In the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ, what do the symbols c and ∆θ stand for?

options.text: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the final temperature
options.rationale: The symbol ∆ means 'change in', so ∆θ is the temperature change, not the final reading.

options.text: c is the specific latent heat and ∆θ is the temperature change
options.rationale: In this equation c is the specific heat capacity; specific latent heat is L in E = m L.

options.text: c is the specific heat capacity and ∆θ is the temperature change
options.rationale: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, c is specific heat capacity in J/kg °C and ∆θ is the temperature change in °C.

options.text: c is the capacity of the container and ∆θ is a state change
options.rationale: Neither symbol refers to the container, and this equation is not used for changes of state.

mcqs.stem: In which of these situations does the equation ∆E = m c ∆θ apply?

options.text: While ice at 0 °C melts into water that is also at 0 °C
options.rationale: There is no temperature change during melting, so E = m L is the equation needed.

options.text: While water at 100 °C is boiling away steadily into steam
options.rationale: Boiling is a change of state at constant temperature, so specific latent heat is used.

options.text: While water at 0 °C freezes solid inside a freezer
options.rationale: Freezing is a change of state, so the energy transferred is found from E = m L.

options.text: While the water in a kettle warms from 20 °C up to 90 °C
options.rationale: The temperature of the water is changing with no change of state, which is when ∆E = m c ∆θ applies.

mcqs.stem: In ∆E = m c ∆θ, which units does the specification give for ∆E and for ∆θ?

options.text: ∆E is in joules, J, and ∆θ is in degrees Celsius, °C
options.rationale: The specification gives change in thermal energy, ∆E, in joules, J, and temperature change, ∆θ, in degrees Celsius, °C.

options.text: ∆E in joules per second, and ∆θ in degrees Celsius, °C
options.rationale: Joules per second is the unit of power; ∆E is an amount of energy in joules.

options.text: ∆E in joules, and ∆θ in joules per kilogram, J/kg
options.rationale: J/kg is the unit of specific latent heat, not of a temperature change.

options.text: ∆E in joules, and ∆θ in J/kg °C
options.rationale: Student thinks the latent-heat unit J/kg °C (m09) belongs on the temperature change.

mcqs.stem: A student uses ∆E = m c ∆θ for a 250 g block of aluminium. What should be substituted for m?

options.text: 250, because that is the mass given in the question
options.rationale: That leaves the mass in grams, which makes the calculated energy 1000 times too large.

options.text: 0.25, because the mass must be in kilograms
options.rationale: Mass, m, is in kilograms, so 250 g is divided by 1000 to give 0.25 kg.

options.text: 2.50, because grams are converted by dividing by 100
options.rationale: There are 1000 grams in a kilogram, not 100, so this conversion is out by a factor of ten.

options.text: 250 000, since kilograms are the larger unit here
options.rationale: Multiplying makes the mass larger, but a 250 g block is less than one kilogram.

mcqs.stem: What are the units of specific heat capacity, and why does a temperature appear in them?

options.text: J/kg, because the value is quoted for one kilogram of substance
options.rationale: J/kg is the unit of specific latent heat; specific heat capacity also fixes a one degree rise.

options.text: J/°C, because the value is quoted for one degree Celsius
options.rationale: This drops the per kilogram condition, which is what the word 'specific' supplies.

options.text: J/kg °C, because the substance is heated for one whole minute
options.rationale: The units are right but the reason is not: no time condition appears in the definition.

options.text: J/kg °C, because the value fixes one kilogram and a one degree rise
options.rationale: Specific heat capacity, c, is in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C, matching its definition.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific heat capacity of a substance?

options.text: The energy required to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
options.rationale: This is the definition: the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius.

options.text: The energy required to raise the whole of the sample by one degree Celsius
options.rationale: The definition fixes the mass at one kilogram; 'specific' means per kilogram.

options.text: The energy required to change the state of one kilogram of it
options.rationale: That is the definition of specific latent heat, where no temperature change occurs.

options.text: The energy stored by one kilogram of it at a given temperature
options.rationale: Specific heat capacity is about energy needed for a change, not energy already stored.

mcqs.stem: Blocks P and Q have the same mass. P has the higher specific heat capacity. The same energy is supplied to each block. What happens?

options.text: P has the greater temperature rise, because its capacity is larger
options.rationale: A larger specific heat capacity means more energy is needed per degree, so the rise is smaller.

options.text: Q has the greater temperature rise, needing less energy per °C
options.rationale: Q needs fewer joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, so the same energy raises its temperature more.

options.text: Both rise by the same amount, since the energy supplied is equal
options.rationale: The type of material affects the rise as well as the mass and the energy supplied.

options.text: Q must change state first, because its capacity is smaller
options.rationale: Specific heat capacity says nothing about whether a change of state happens.

mcqs.stem: 10 500 J are supplied to 0.50 kg of water, which does not boil. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the temperature change?

options.rationale: This leaves the mass out, as if the specific heat capacity applied to the whole sample rather than to each kilogram.
This comes from multiplying by the mass instead of dividing by it when the equation is rearranged.
This comes from substituting the mass as 500 g rather than converting it to 0.50 kg.

mcqs.stem: 10 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. What is the change in thermal energy?

options.rationale: This is the result of leaving the mass out of the calculation.
This comes from using 4.2 in place of 4200, a slip made when grams and kilograms are mixed.
This comes from dividing by the mass instead of multiplying by it.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the latent heat of a substance?

options.text: The energy stored by a substance once it has melted
options.rationale: Latent heat is the energy needed to make the change happen, not a store left behind afterwards.

options.text: The energy that is needed for a substance to change state
options.rationale: The specification calls the energy needed for a substance to change state its latent heat.

options.text: The energy needed to raise a substance by one degree
options.rationale: That is about specific heat capacity, which applies when the temperature changes.

options.text: The energy lost by a substance while its temperature is constant
options.rationale: Energy is supplied to the substance during melting or boiling; it is not lost.

mcqs.stem: Steam is produced steadily from boiling water at 100 °C. What happens to the energy that is supplied?

options.text: It raises the temperature of the water past 100 °C
options.rationale: While the change of state is happening the temperature stays at the boiling point.

options.text: It is stored in the heater until the boiling has finished
options.rationale: The energy is transferred to the water, where it produces the change of state.

options.text: It changes the energy stored but not the temperature
options.rationale: During a change of state the energy supplied changes the internal energy of the substance, not its temperature.

options.text: It leaves the water's own internal energy unchanged
options.rationale: A constant temperature does not mean a constant internal energy; the potential energy store is rising.

mcqs.stem: Which energy store of the particles increases while a solid melts at constant temperature?

options.text: Their kinetic energy, because the particles must be moving faster
options.rationale: Faster particles would show as a rising temperature, and the temperature is constant.

options.text: Their thermal energy, as heat flows into the solid and is stored
options.rationale: Caloric view: heat is a substance that flows in and is stored, so 'heat energy' rises.

options.text: Neither store, because the temperature is not changing at all
options.rationale: Internal energy does rise during a change of state even though the temperature does not.

options.text: Their potential energy, as the particles are pulled apart
options.rationale: The energy supplied separates the particles against the forces between them, raising their potential energy store.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is the specification definition of the specific latent heat of a substance?

options.text: The energy needed to change the state of a whole sample of it
options.rationale: The definition is fixed at one kilogram; that is what the word 'specific' adds.

options.text: The energy to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
options.rationale: This is the definition: the energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.

options.text: The energy needed to raise one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
options.rationale: That is the definition of specific heat capacity, not of specific latent heat.

options.text: The energy needed to change one kilogram of it by one degree Celsius
options.rationale: A change of state happens with no change in temperature, so no degree Celsius condition belongs here.

mcqs.stem: Which equation gives the energy needed for a change of state?

options.text: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat × ∆θ
options.rationale: There is no temperature change during a change of state, so no ∆θ term belongs in this equation.

options.text: energy for a state change = mass ÷ specific latent heat
options.rationale: The quantities are multiplied: E = m L, so twice the mass needs twice the energy.

options.text: energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat
options.rationale: This is the specification equation, written in symbols as E = m L.

options.text: energy for a change of state = mass × specific heat capacity
options.rationale: Specific heat capacity belongs to the equation used when the temperature changes.

mcqs.stem: The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is 330 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 0.30 kg of ice that is already at 0 °C?

options.rationale: This is a place-value slip in multiplying 330 000 by 0.30, giving an answer ten times too small.
This comes from dividing the specific latent heat by the mass instead of multiplying.
This comes from substituting the mass as 300 g rather than converting it to 0.30 kg.

mcqs.stem: In E = m L, which units does the specification give for the three quantities?

options.text: E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram
options.rationale: The specification gives energy, E, in joules, J; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; specific latent heat, L, in joules per kilogram, J/kg.

options.text: E in joules, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram per °C
options.rationale: J/kg °C is the unit of specific heat capacity; there is no temperature change here.

options.text: E in joules, m in grams, L in joules per kilogram of substance
options.rationale: Mass in these equations is in kilograms, not grams.

options.text: E in joules per second, m in kilograms, L in joules per kilogram
options.rationale: Joules per second is power; E here is an amount of energy in joules.

mcqs.stem: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of fusion describe?

options.text: The change of state from liquid to vapour, that is boiling
options.rationale: That change is described by the specific latent heat of vaporisation.

options.text: The change of state from a solid straight to a vapour
options.rationale: Thinking fusion turns the solid into a gas, the student picks solid-straight-to-vapour.

options.text: The change of state from a solid to a liquid, that is melting
options.rationale: The specification gives specific latent heat of fusion as the change of state from solid to liquid.

options.text: The change of state from liquid into a warmer liquid
options.rationale: Warming a liquid is a temperature change, handled by specific heat capacity, not a change of state.

mcqs.stem: Which change of state does the specific latent heat of vaporisation describe?

options.text: The change of state from a solid straight into a gas
options.rationale: Believing latent heat is about becoming a gas, the student picks the solid-to-gas option.

options.text: The change of state from solid to liquid
options.rationale: That change is described by the specific latent heat of fusion.

options.text: The rise in temperature of the vapour formed
options.rationale: A temperature rise is dealt with by specific heat capacity, not by specific latent heat.

options.text: The change of state from a liquid to a vapour
options.rationale: The specification gives specific latent heat of vaporisation as the change of state from liquid to vapour.

mcqs.stem: A solid is heated at a steady rate and a graph of temperature against time is plotted. What does a flat section of the graph show?

options.text: The substance is changing state while energy is supplied
options.rationale: A flat section means constant temperature: the energy supplied is producing the change of state.

options.text: The substance has reached the hottest temperature it can ever reach
options.rationale: The temperature climbs again once the change of state is complete, so this is not a ceiling.

options.text: The heater has been switched off, so no energy is transferred
options.rationale: The heater is still supplying energy; only the temperature has stopped changing.

options.text: The substance is warming too slowly for the thermometer
options.rationale: The temperature really is constant; the instrument is not at fault.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes specific heat capacity from specific latent heat?

options.text: They are two names for one quantity, so either may be used for any change
options.rationale: They are different quantities, with different units and different equations.

options.text: Specific heat capacity needs a temperature change; latent heat does not
options.rationale: c is the energy per kilogram per degree Celsius of temperature change; L is the energy per kilogram to change state at constant temperature.

options.text: Specific heat capacity changes state; specific latent heat changes temperature
options.rationale: The two have been swapped: c is for a temperature change and L is for a change of state.

options.text: Either quantity may be used for any thermal change at all
options.rationale: Treating the two as one interchangeable quantity usable for any thermal change.
